chapter: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
title: Overwork and copying Strayhorn's symphony in 1968
summary: Whaley recalls tearing up music at the Lafayette, and sitting eleven hours copying a Strayhorn symphony in 1968 and being unable to move afterwards.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: So I said, go ahead, it's your show and I tore up all the music. Then I had to go back and write it.. That's why I'm blind today.
You really work hard writing that music.

In '68 I sat up 11 hours writing and when I got through -- because I was writing a symphony for Billy Strayhorn, see, copying that symphony and when I got through, I threw the pen down and said, that's it, and I sat on the couch and you know, I couldn't move. I couldn't move and I called the doctor up, I got to the phone and called Dr. Logan up, and Logan said well, get in some hot water and I got in hot water, you know, I couldn't walk for a year and a half. Right. It's too much work, sitting there.
Do you remember the name of the symphony. What Strayhorn called it.
What did he call it. It was some of Strayhorn's work. He put it all together.
Where did he do it, did he do it here or in Europe.
They did it -- I don't think they did it, because I ain't never heard it, see.
If I had some of it here, would you notice any of it of yours.
No, I wouldn't know it, no.
